analysis.title: How the blue wave could reshape US energy and data centres
key_insights: Exit polls from the 2026 US midterms show energy affordability shaped the vote: nearly 90% of voters called cost of living a crucial or major factor, and 56% said the AI data centre boom's strain on power supply was a crucial or major factor.

Democrats are set to control both the House and Senate with a Republican White House. ING expects the divided government to focus on shielding consumers from data centre power costs, speeding new power supply through permitting reform, and protecting supply chains.
More aggressive legislation risks a veto from President Trump, so ING considers sweeping data centre legislation unlikely.

Data centre regulation is likely to tighten mainly at the state level: data centre taxes, reduced tax incentives, environmental standards, and requirements for developers to bear cost increases. Outright moratoriums are unlikely to become mainstream and would more likely be temporary.

At the federal level, action is more likely to focus on protecting electricity customers from higher costs and formalising data centres' responsibility to fund grid and energy infrastructure upgrades. These could ride on must-pass spending bills or a permitting reform package.

ING expects Democrats to increase scrutiny of technology companies and use the next two years to prepare an AI governance framework for 2028 and beyond. Tighter AI and data centre regulation is unlikely to change the industry's growth trajectory, given AI's importance to US growth and competition with China.

Stricter state rules could slow project development but raise the value of data centres already approved or under construction, easing capital constraints and pushing developers toward more measured expansion.
Surveys show 20-30% of Americans support local data centre construction, rising to 50-70% with community investments. More developers are signing binding community benefit agreements.

Both parties support faster expansion of electricity supply. Nuclear, geothermal, carbon capture and biofuels are likely to keep bipartisan support, but permitting reform offers the greatest scope for policy action.
Many energy projects spend over five years in federal permitting. About $240bn-$280bn of infrastructure investment enters the permitting pipeline each year across eight sectors.

The Senate introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) in September 2026 and is expected to vote on 9 November. It would still need House and presidential approval. Delaying it until Democrats regain control next year would raise the risk of a veto, which gives both sides an incentive to deal sooner.
If enacted, BAAJA could significantly shorten permitting timelines for renewables and fossil fuel projects, reduce litigation and permit cancellation risk, and widen project siting options.

Reducing reliance on China for clean energy technologies and critical minerals will remain a US priority. ING expects this to raise project costs near term, with possible long-term benefits from stronger domestic manufacturing and more secure supply chains.

The executive branch could add protective measures with little opposition from Congress. A Democratic Congress could push to extend clean manufacturing tax credits as part of a broader deal with Trump.
Solar could face particular cost pressures because some tariffs on supply chain equipment also apply to non-Chinese suppliers.

The US is supporting rare earth production in Australia and Brazil. Solar and battery suppliers in South Korea and Japan could benefit. European clean energy developers could face more competition for non-Chinese supplies.

sector_views.rationale: State-level regulation could slow project development in tight states but raise the value of approved or under-construction projects. Growth trajectory is unlikely to change fundamentally.
BAAJA permitting reform, if enacted, could significantly shorten timelines and reduce litigation and cancellation risk.
Domestic manufacturing is supported by China-focused trade and tax credit restrictions, but some tariffs also hit non-Chinese suppliers and raise costs.
US funding, purchase agreements and equity investments support domestic production, and the policy focus is expected to continue.

risk_factors: Presidential veto of aggressive data centre or energy legislation.
Delay of BAAJA until the next Congress, which raises veto risk.
Near-term cost increases from onshoring and supply chain diversification.
Local opposition and state-level rules slowing data centre project siting.
Tariffs on supply chain equipment raising solar costs, including for non-Chinese suppliers.
geopolitical: US-China competition over supply chains for clean energy technologies and critical minerals, including Chinese export restrictions on rare earths that contributed to disruptions for US auto manufacturers.
US support for rare earth production in Australia and Brazil.
EU tightening restrictions on Chinese equipment through funding, procurement, auction and subsidy rules.

tension_points.bull_case: Both parties see a need for permitting reform, and the veto risk gives Democrats an incentive to pass BAAJA now, which would shorten timelines and cut litigation risk.
tension_points.bear_case: Democrats may delay the bill to seek changes once they control Congress next year, which could increase the risk of a presidential veto.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The Senate vote expected on 9 November, followed by House and presidential approval, decides whether BAAJA becomes law in this Congress.

theme_stances.key_argument: Targeted state-level regulation and federal affordability measures are likely, but sweeping legislation is unlikely given Trump's veto power.
theme_stances.evidence: sweeping data centre legislation is unlikely because of President Trump's veto power

theme_stances.key_argument: There is broad agreement that BAAJA would meaningfully improve the permitting process, and both parties have an incentive to deal sooner.
theme_stances.evidence: broad agreement that the BAAJA would meaningfully improve the permitting process
